candidates.name: Make the Upsell a Tracked, Incentivized Habit
candidates.mechanism: Asking staff to 'upsell more' rarely works on its own — it's vague, untracked, and easy to forget in the moment. Giving staff a specific, structured prompt to offer at the right moment, with a visible, real-time incentive tied to it, turns an occasional ad-lib pitch into a repeatable habit.
candidates.evidence: Clarion Hotel Sign (Stockholm) implemented a front-desk upselling system that prompts staff with structured room-upgrade and add-on offers at check-in, with real-time commission tracking to keep staff motivated. The hotel saw a 381% increase in upsell revenue in the first few months, reaching an average of €47.57 in upsell revenue per guest.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of a general 'try to upsell more' reminder, give techs a specific, structured offer to make at a specific moment (e.g. 'while you're here, want us to check the water heater too?' right after diagnosing the main issue), and track and share back with them how often it converts. A vague instruction to sell more gets forgotten; a specific prompt with visible results attached becomes a habit.

candidates.name: Unbundle the Price So Every Extra Is Its Own Yes
candidates.mechanism: When everything is folded into one price, customers never separately decide whether each part is worth paying for — they just accept or reject the whole package. Pulling optional extras out as their own priced line items forces (and enables) a customer to say yes to more of them individually, each of which is easier to agree to than the bundle would have been to upsize.
candidates.evidence: Per the airline industry's own tracked ancillary revenue data (IdeaWorksCompany's Global Estimate of Ancillary Revenue), the ten airlines with the most ancillary revenue collected $54.1 billion in 2023, up from $38.4 billion in 2019 — extras like seat selection, baggage, and onboard purchases sold separately from the base fare, adding up to a large and fast-growing share of total revenue industry-wide.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of quoting one all-in number, itemize the optional extras on the quote as their own line items the customer can add or skip individually — a filter upgrade, an extended warranty, a follow-up inspection. Bundled into one price, most customers never separately consider whether each piece is worth it; broken out, each becomes its own small, easy yes.
candidates.verificationCaveats: The aggregate ancillary revenue figures ($38.4B in 2019 to $54.1B in 2023) are real and verified directly against the source. The specific mechanism claimed here — that unbundling makes each extra 'its own easy yes' for the customer — is an inference drawn from that data, not something the source itself states or measures directly.

candidates.name: Bundle It Into One Easy, Good-Value Choice
candidates.mechanism: Asking a customer to separately decide on several add-ons creates several chances to say no. Pre-bundling complementary items into one simple, visibly-discounted choice removes that friction — it's one easy decision instead of three small ones, and it reliably increases what the average customer walks out having bought.
candidates.evidence: McDonald's brought back its Extra Value Meals combo platform in 2025 (main item plus sides and a drink, priced at roughly a 15% discount versus ordering the same items separately); the platform grew to about 30% of U.S. transactions and the company attributed a 2.4% same-store sales increase in Q3 2025 primarily to an increase in average check size.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of listing the core job and then asking separately about each add-on, offer one pre-bundled package that combines the job with the couple of things most customers end up wanting anyway (e.g. 'repair + filter change + tune-up' as a single line, priced a bit below what all three would cost separately). One easy yes to a good-value bundle converts more often than three separate asks.
